name: Chang'e 2
short_status: Mapped the Moon at 7 m through 2011, reached Sun-Earth L2, flew by asteroid Toutatis Dec 13, 2012; contact faded after 2014, now a silent derelict in solar orbit.
tagline: CNSA · China · Orbiter · 2010 · The robotic return Success
stats: resolution of its full-Moon map, the sharpest complete lunar map published to that date (Feb 2012)
closest approach to asteroid Toutatis (plus or minus 120 m), measured from the surface
relative speed of the Toutatis flyby
destinations on one spacecraft: lunar orbit, Sun-Earth L2, and an asteroid

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1 October 2010, 10:59:57 UTC, Long March 3C from Xichang Satellite Launch Center LC-2

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: 2,480 kg on the DFH-3 series bus (DFH-3A in Gunter's listing), flown from Chang'e 1's backup hardware with upgraded instruments; six-month design life

facts.label: Camera
facts.value: Three-line-array CCD stereo camera: 10 m resolution from the 100 km orbit, 1.5 m from the 15 km perilune passes

facts.label: Chang'e 3 site reconnaissance
facts.value: Perilune lowered to 15 km on 26 October 2010 for meter-class imaging of Sinus Iridum, the then-planned Chang'e 3 landing region

facts.label: Global map
facts.value: 7 m per pixel full-Moon map released 6 February 2012, built from over 700 frames taken October 2010 to May 2011; announced by SASTIND as the highest-resolution published map of the entire lunar surface to that date

facts.label: Sun-Earth L2 record
facts.value: Arrived 25 August 2011 after a 77-day cruise: the first spacecraft to reach Sun-Earth L2 directly from lunar orbit

facts.label: Toutatis flyby
facts.value: 13 December 2012: closest approach 770 plus or minus 120 m from the asteroid's surface at 10.73 km/s relative speed

facts.label: Flyby camera
facts.value: A small engineering camera installed to monitor the solar panel, with a 1024-pixel-square detector shooting up to 5 frames per second, took the flyby images instead of the lunar mapping camera

facts.label: Flyby conditions
facts.value: Encounter occurred more than 7 million km from Earth, over 20 times the design range of the communication system, on a 20 kb/s downlink through the probe's 0.6 m antenna

facts.label: Toutatis results
facts.value: Images better than 3 m resolution showed a bifurcated contact binary about 4.75 x 1.95 km (plus or minus 10 percent) with a giant basin at the big end and boulders and regolith suggesting a rubble-pile structure

facts.label: Asteroid first
facts.value: First Chinese asteroid encounter; China became the fourth space agency to study an asteroid up close, after the United States, Europe, and Japan

facts.label: Deep-space coda
facts.value: China's national space science data center lists the spacecraft more than 200 million km from Earth as of 2016, with the extended cruise used to exercise the country's deep-space tracking network

timeline: Launched on a Long March 3C from Xichang on China's National Day, riding the country's first direct translunar trajectory
Braked into lunar orbit after a transfer of under five days
Settled into the 100 km circular polar working orbit
Perilune dropped to 15 km; low passes image Sinus Iridum, the planned Chang'e 3 landing region, at meter scale
First Sinus Iridum close-ups published in Beijing
Fires its engine and departs lunar orbit for Sun-Earth L2, its primary mapping mission complete
Arrives at Sun-Earth L2 after a 77-day cruise, the first spacecraft to reach it directly from lunar orbit
SASTIND releases the 7 m per pixel map of the entire Moon assembled from Chang'e 2 imagery
Leaves L2 on an eight-month intercept of near-Earth asteroid 4179 Toutatis
Flies past Toutatis at 770 plus or minus 120 m and 10.73 km/s, more than 7 million km from Earth: China's first asteroid encounter
Tracked beyond 100 million km from Earth as controllers exercise China's deep-space network
Around 2029
The silent derelict's solar orbit is projected to bring it back through Earth's neighborhood
